title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Take a close look at the surface of this canvas. Do you notice how the paint seems to leap off the fabric? In the depiction of the mother and her youngest child, Rembrandt used a palette knife and thick impasto, creating a texture that feels almost like a relief sculpture. Look for the small basket of flowers held by the daughter; if you peer closely, you will find the artist's signature hidden there.

This painting is shrouded in mystery. We don't know who these people are, nor do we know if they paid for the portrait or if Rembrandt painted them freely. For centuries, the identity of the sitters caused great debate. Until the mid-19th century, many believed this was actually a portrait of Rembrandt and his own family. Given that the artist suffered devastating personal losses—including his wife and children—could this happy scene be a poignant "counter-idyll," a painted dream of a family life he no longer had?

Even the art world couldn't agree on its value. While some early critics dismissed the work as "strange" or a sign of the artist's decline, others, like painter Lovis Corinth, hailed it as a "Brunswick jewel." Today, this is celebrated as one of Rembrandt's final masterpieces. Why do you think the artist chose to strip away all furniture and background details, leaving us with nothing but these figures emerging from the shadows?

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Take a moment to look at this intimate scene by Rembrandt, painted near the end of the artist's life between 1665 and 1668. You are looking at an unknown family: a mother with her youngest child on her lap, a father holding a red flower, and two older children engaged in a quiet conversation. One daughter holds a basket of flowers, where you can find the artist's signature.

Notice how Rembrandt focuses entirely on the people, leaving the background empty. There is no grand furniture or formal posing here; instead, the atmosphere feels warm and happy. While the family remains a mystery, some believe this painting served as a bittersweet contrast to Rembrandt's own life, as he had lost his wife, companion, and several children by the time he painted this.

For a long time, critics found this style strange, but today it is cherished as a masterpiece. It is the most important Rembrandt work in the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum collection. As you explore the painting together, notice the rich reds and browns and the way the figures seem to interact with one another.

Looking at the expressions and the way the family members are positioned, what do you think this painting tells us about the relationship between the people depicted?

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
You are standing before one of the most significant treasures of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum: Rembrandt’s Portrait of a Family. Painted between 1665 and 1668, this is one of the Dutch master's final works and a cornerstone of art history.

What makes this painting truly iconic is its daring style. Look closely at the surface; Rembrandt used a palette knife and thick impasto to create a texture so heavy it almost resembles a relief sculpture. This bold, coarse brushwork was so radical that early critics found the piece strange, even suggesting it showed a decline in his ability. However, later artists, such as Lovis Corinth, hailed it as a jewel.

Today, this painting is celebrated as a bridge to the future. Alongside his late self-portraits, it establishes Rembrandt’s reputation as the first modern painter. By stripping away the lavish furniture and proud poses typical of the era, he focused entirely on the raw emotion of a happy family.

The mystery adds to its allure: the family remains unidentified, and for centuries, people mistakenly believed it was a portrait of Rembrandt's own family. Whether it was a rejected commission or a personal reflection, it remains the museum's most important work by the master. Keep an eye out for the artist's signature on the flower basket—a final, definitive mark from one of the greatest painters to ever live.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Executed between 1665 and 1668, this late work is a study in tactile surface and psychological intimacy. Note the aggressive application of paint; Rembrandt employs thick impasto and a palette knife to create a relief-like texture, particularly in the figures of the mother and youngest child. This coarse brushwork, combined with a palette dominated by browns, greens, and intense reds, marks a departure from the polished finishes of earlier eras.

Compositionally, Rembrandt strips away all representative elements. There is no furniture or architectural detail to define the space, focusing the viewer entirely on the familial interaction. While the painting was acquired by Duke Anton Ulrich of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, the identities of the sitters remain unknown. This ambiguity fuels scholarly debate: some suggest the work was a commission rejected by the patrons, while others interpret it as a counter-idyll to Rembrandt's own tragic domestic life following the deaths of his wife Saskia, partner Hendrickje Stoffels, and son Titus.

Historically, the reception of this piece has shifted dramatically. Once dismissed as evidence of declining skill, it is now championed as a masterly late work. Alongside The Jewish Bride and his final self-portraits, this painting documents Rembrandt's evolution into what some art historians call the first modern painter. The work is signed on the flower basket as Rembrandt f, though it remains undated, serving as a pivotal example of the artist's late-period exploration of form and emotion.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Take a moment to let the world outside fade away and simply be present with this scene. Before you is a quiet, intimate encounter between a mother, a father, and their three children. Notice how the room disappears into a soft, dark void, leaving only the family in a pool of warm, enveloping light.

Observe the gentle interactions: the youngest child resting securely in its mother's lap, and the siblings turned toward one another in a hushed, private conversation. Even the father, standing slightly behind them, holds a single red flower, adding a touch of tenderness to the stillness.

Allow your eyes to wander over the surface of the canvas. The paint is applied with a rich, tactile thickness, creating a relief that feels almost sculptural, especially in the embrace between mother and child. The deep browns, greens, and intense reds create an atmosphere of profound warmth and security.

As you stand in this silence, let the painting invite you into its sense of harmony and peace. There are no grand gestures here, no proud poses—only the simple, enduring beauty of a happy family. Reflect on the quiet bonds of love and protection depicted here. What does this stillness evoke within you? Let the warmth of the colors and the intimacy of the scene offer you a moment of restoration and calm.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Observe the surface of this canvas, likely painted between 1665 and 1668. This is one of Rembrandt's final works, and it demonstrates a daring, experimental approach to oil painting. Notice how the paint is applied with thick impasto and coarse brushwork, and in some areas, the artist used a palette knife. Look closely at the mother and her youngest child; the paint is so heavily layered that the figures almost emerge as a three-dimensional relief.

Rembrandt eschews all traditional markers of status. There is no splendid furniture, no proud posing, and the background is entirely obscured, stripping away everything but the human connection. The palette is restricted to earthy browns, greens, and intense reds, which focus your attention on the intimate interactions: the two older children in conversation and the father holding a single red flower.

For centuries, this style was misunderstood. Until the early 20th century, critics viewed the work as strange or a sign of declining skill. However, modern art historians now see this as a masterly late work. By abandoning the polished finish of his contemporaries in favor of raw texture and emotional immediacy, Rembrandt established himself as a precursor to modern painting. While the identities of this family remain a mystery, the work stands as the most important Rembrandt in the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, capturing a quiet, happy atmosphere through a revolutionary application of paint.

text:

At first glance, it is a simple image of a happy family: a mother with her youngest child on her lap, two older children chatting, and a father holding a single red flower in the background. But look closer at the surface of the canvas. Do you see how the paint is piled up, almost like a relief sculpture? Rembrandt used a palette knife and thick brushwork to create this texture, especially on the mother and child.

This painting is one of Rembrandt's final works, created between 1665 and 1668. For a long time, people believed this was a portrait of the artist's own family, but today we know the identities of these people remain a mystery. It is an intriguing puzzle: was this a commissioned work that the clients rejected, or a personal project? Some suggest it was a "counter-idyll," a dream of family happiness painted while Rembrandt was facing profound personal loss.

The painting's history is just as surprising. While it is now the most important Rembrandt in this museum, critics in the early 20th century once called it strange, even suggesting it showed the artist's skills were fading. Now, it is celebrated as a masterpiece of modern painting. Can you find the artist's signature? It is hidden on the basket of flowers. As you look at the figures, ask yourself: what stories do you think are being shared between the children?

While it captures a seemingly happy family, this work is a masterpiece of mystery. The identities of the couple and their children remain unknown. For centuries, the painting’s reputation shifted wildly. Until the early 20th century, some critics dismissed it as strange or a sign of the artist's decline. Yet, others saw a "jewel," recognizing in these bold strokes the birth of a modern style.

Now, look for the small basket of flowers held by the daughter; that is where you will find Rembrandt's signature. Created between 1665 and 1668, this was one of the last works of the master's life. It is a painting of profound contradictions: it celebrates a joyful family scene, yet it was painted while Rembrandt suffered immense personal loss, including the deaths of his wives and children.

Today, this is regarded as the most important Rembrandt in the museum's collection. It is a cornerstone of art history, marking the transition to modern painting. If you are looking for the essence of Rembrandt's late genius, you have found it here—in the bold textures and the enduring mystery of these anonymous faces.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Look closely at the surface of this canvas, likely painted between 1665 and 1668. This is one of Rembrandt's final works, and it reveals a daring approach to oil painting. Notice the heavy impasto and coarse brushwork, particularly on the mother and youngest child. In these areas, the paint is applied so thickly—partly with a palette knife—that the image takes on the quality of a relief.

The composition is strikingly minimalist. By omitting furniture or architectural details, Rembrandt focuses entirely on the emotional bond of the unidentified couple and their three children. Can you spot the artist's signature? It is tucked away on the flower basket held by the daughter.

The history of this painting is as layered as its paint. For centuries, it was a subject of debate. Until the early 20th century, some critics dismissed it as "strange," viewing the loose style as a sign of declining skill. Others, like painter Lovis Corinth, hailed it as a jewel. For a time, it was even believed to be a portrait of Rembrandt's own family, perhaps serving as a poignant counter-idyll to his personal tragedies, including the loss of his wife and children.

Today, scholars view this work as a precursor to modern painting. It leaves us with an enduring mystery: was this a commissioned piece that the clients rejected, or a free exploration of domestic happiness? Consider this alongside the late self-portraits and The Jewish Bride to see how Rembrandt redefined the boundaries of his era.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Take a moment to let the bustle of the gallery fade away and simply look at this family. Notice how Rembrandt has stripped away everything unnecessary—there is no furniture, no lavish setting, no proud posing. There is only the intimacy of these five people.

As you look closer, observe the texture of the paint. In the depiction of the mother and her youngest child, the paint is applied so thickly that it becomes almost like a relief, a physical presence you can almost feel. Follow the gaze of the children as they whisper to one another, and see the father in the background, quietly holding a single red flower.

The history of this painting is a mystery. We do not know who these people were, or if they were even real. For a long time, it was believed to be a portrait of Rembrandt's own family—perhaps a longing for a happiness that had slipped away, as he suffered the loss of his wife and children.

Let the oddity of this work invite you to be curious. In the early 20th century, some found this style strange, even failing, yet others saw it as a jewel. Today, it is celebrated as a bridge to modern art.

As you stand here, ask yourself: what does it mean to be truly seen by another? Can you find the small, hidden signature on the flower basket? Let the silence of this family inspire your own sense of discovery.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Standing before you is one of the final masterpieces by the Dutch legend Rembrandt, painted between 1665 and 1668. This is the Portrait of a Family, a work that captures a moment of quiet, domestic happiness.

Take a look at the surface. You will see an incredible use of thick, textured paint—some of it applied with a palette knife—that makes the figures almost pop out like a relief. This bold style is exactly why some early critics found the painting strange, while others, like the artist Lovis Corinth, called it a jewel.

The painting is a critical piece of art history because it marks Rembrandt's transition into what many call the first modern painter. Rather than painting proud poses or lavish furniture, he focused entirely on the emotional connection between the people.

While the identities of the family remain a mystery, the painting is a centerpiece of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, which considers it the most important Rembrandt in its collection. Look closely at the basket of flowers held by the daughter; that is where you will find the artist's signature.

As you admire this scene, consider the contrast between the warmth on the canvas and the tragedy of Rembrandt's own life, as he had lost his wife and children by the time he painted this. It is a powerful testament to his ability to evoke a feeling of love and belonging.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Painted between 1665 and 1668, this oil on canvas is one of Rembrandt’s final works. It captures an unknown family of five, stripped of the typical status symbols of the era. Notice how the artist avoids splendid furniture or formal poses, focusing entirely on the figures to create a sense of domestic happiness.

Take a close look at the composition and point out the details. You can see the youngest child on the mother's lap and a daughter holding a basket of flowers, which bears the artist's signature. The father stands slightly behind the group, holding a single red flower.

The painting is a masterclass in late-period Rembrandt. He uses a palette of browns, greens, and intense reds, applying the paint with a thick, heavy impasto. In the depiction of the mother and child, the paint is so raised it almost resembles a relief sculpture.

The history of the work is as intriguing as the image. While once titled Rembrandt with His Family, the identities of the sitters remain a mystery. Some historians suggest it was a commissioned work that was never accepted by the clients, while others see it as a poignant counter-idyll to the tragedies of Rembrandt's own personal life. 

Once dismissed by critics as a sign of declining skill, it is now celebrated as a modern masterpiece. Alongside the late self-portraits and The Jewish Bride, this work cements Rembrandt's legacy as a pioneer of modern painting.

As you stand here, let the silence of the painting speak to you. Perhaps you can imagine the hushed tones of the children's conversation or the quiet pride in the father's gaze. Consider the feeling of this scene as a whole. What does this image suggest to you about the nature of love and kinship? Let your eyes wander across the canvas and find a place where you feel a sense of peace.

title: Portrait of a Family
text:
Executed between 1665 and 1668, this oil on canvas is one of Rembrandt's final works and a cornerstone of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum's collection. While the identities of the couple and their three children remain a mystery, the painting's significance lies in its bold, modern execution.

Rembrandt eschews traditional markers of status, omitting lavish furniture or formal poses to focus entirely on the family's intimacy. Note the dramatic application of paint; the artist used a palette knife and thick impasto, particularly on the mother and child, creating a tactile, relief-like surface. This coarse brushwork is a hallmark of his late style.

The work's reception has evolved dramatically. Until the early 20th century, some critics viewed its unconventional style as a sign of declining ability. Today, however, it is celebrated as a masterly achievement. Alongside works like The Jewish Bride and his late self-portraits, this piece supports the view of Rembrandt as the first modern painter.

One intriguing point of debate is whether this was a commissioned piece or a personal project. Given that it was once titled Rembrandt with His Family, some interpret it as a counter-idyll to the artist's own tragic personal losses, including the deaths of his wives and children. Whether a commission or a reflection of longing, the painting is now regarded as a jewel of Dutch art, documenting a pivotal shift toward the expressive freedom of modern painting.

Observe the handling of the paint; the artist used a palette knife and thick impasto to create a surface that feels almost like a relief, particularly where the mother holds her youngest child.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Look closely at this 1659 scene by Johannes Vermeer. While the luminous red dress of the young woman immediately grabs your attention, the real mysteries lie in the periphery. Notice the man in the far left corner. Has he simply fallen asleep, or is he a drunken husband, blissfully unaware that the young man beside him is attempting to seduce his wife?

Scan the background for a dark, shadowed portrait on the wall. Could this be the absent husband, watching the scene with a silent, admonishing gaze? Even the objects on the table hold clues; consider the citrus fruits and the liquid in the glass. Is it merely wine, or perhaps an aphrodisiac intended to fuel the encounter?

Now, shift your gaze to the leaded glass window on the left. If you look very closely at the colored coat of arms, you can find an allegory of Temperantia, the virtue of Temperance. Why would Vermeer place a symbol of restraint in a room filled with seduction and intoxication?

This painting, now in the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, has traveled from the private collection of a Duke in the 17th century to a modern German postage stamp. As you stand before it, ask yourself: who is the true protagonist of this story? Is it the embarrassed girl looking toward us, the persistent suitor, or the silent observer in the portrait?

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted by Johannes Vermeer between 1658 and 1659, this scene invites us to uncover a silent story. In the center, a young woman in a luminous red dress holds a wine glass. Notice how her bright clothing makes her stand out from everything else in the room. A young man leans toward her, holding her hand as if urging her to drink. Meanwhile, in the back corner, a second man has fallen asleep behind a table set with a wine jug and fruit.

Look closely at the surroundings together. On the wall hangs a dark portrait of a man, and to the left, there is a leaded glass window featuring a colored coat of arms. This window depicts Temperance, one of the cardinal virtues, which provides a sharp contrast to the scene unfolding before us.

The painting is full of mystery. Is the sleeping man a drunken husband, oblivious to the young man's attempt to seduce the girl? Is the man in the portrait watching over her in admonition? The girl herself looks toward us with an expression of embarrassment, as if she has just been caught.

Take a moment to look at the three characters and the portrait. Based on their expressions and positions, what do you think is actually happening in this room, and who do you think the man in the portrait is?

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
You are standing before one of the most captivating works by the Dutch master Johannes Vermeer, a painter whose rare talent has made his pieces some of the most sought-after treasures in the world. Painted between 1658 and 1659, The Girl with the Wine Glass is a masterpiece of tension and storytelling.

Notice the striking contrast of the girl's luminous red dress against the muted tones of the room. This bold use of color draws your eye immediately to the center of a provocative scene: a young man leans in, urging her to drink, while another man slumbers in the background. The mystery of the painting lies in its hidden meanings. Is the sleeping man a drunken husband? Is the portrait on the wall a silent warning? Even the window holds a secret, featuring the allegory of Temperance, a cardinal virtue that stands in direct contrast to the seductive atmosphere of the room.

This painting is so iconic that it has transcended the walls of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum, appearing on official German postage stamps as a national treasure. Its ability to freeze a moment of psychological drama in time is exactly why Vermeer remains a titan of art history. As you move on, remember this image of the girl looking back at you in embarrassment—it is one of the most enduring and shareable moments of the Dutch Golden Age.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted between 1658 and 1659, this oil on canvas is a quintessential Dutch genre picture. The composition is anchored by a striking chromatic contrast: the luminous red of the girl's dress serves as the focal point, sharply juxtaposed against the muted, pale palette of the men's clothing and the surrounding interior.

The narrative depth of the work invites scholarly debate regarding its moral subtext. Note the tension between the figures: a young man leans in, urging the girl to drink, while a second man sits dazed in the background, seemingly succumbed to intoxication. The presence of citrus fruits on the table suggests the drink may be an aphrodisiac rather than simple wine. This tension is further complicated by the portrait on the wall—perhaps an absent or admonishing husband—and the stained glass window, which features an allegory of Temperantia, the virtue of temperance.

Johannes Vermeer uses these symbolic elements to create a complex scene of seduction and moral warning. The interaction of light and shadow, particularly the darkness falling across the background portrait, enhances this psychological layering. Provenance records show the work was acquired around 1696 by Anton Ulrich, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, and it remains a cornerstone of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum. When analyzing this piece, consider how Vermeer uses the architectural elements of the room and the specific placement of the figures to direct the viewer's eye toward these conflicting themes of desire and restraint.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Take a moment to let your eyes wander through this quiet, tension-filled room. Your gaze is immediately drawn to the girl in the center, wearing a luminous red dress that vibrates against the pale, muted tones of the interior. She holds a wine glass, but her expression is one of hesitation; she looks sideways toward you, as if seeking an escape from the scene.

Notice the young man leaning toward her, holding her hand and urging her to drink. Is this a simple gesture of courtship, or something more calculating? In the background, a second man has fallen asleep behind a table set with a wine jug and fruit. He may be a drunken husband, oblivious to the seduction taking place right in front of him.

Look closer at the wall behind them. A dark portrait of a man hangs in the shadows, his gaze acting as a silent admonition. Even more subtle is the leaded glass window to the left. If you look at the coat of arms in the center, you can recognize the allegory of Temperantia, the virtue of Temperance. 

Vermeer leaves the true nature of the encounter ambiguous. Is the liquid in the glass simple wine, or an aphrodisiac suggested by the citrus fruits on the table? As you stand here, you are the only witness to this private drama, caught between the sleeping man, the watching portrait, and the girl's embarrassed glance.

Nehmen Sie sich einen Moment Zeit und lassen Sie Ihren Blick durch diesen stillen, spannungsgeladenen Raum wandern. Ihr Blick fällt sofort auf das Mädchen in der Mitte, in einem leuchtend roten Kleid, das vor den blassen, gedämpften Tönen des Raumes förmlich vibriert. Sie hält ein Weinglas, doch ihr Ausdruck ist zögernd; sie blickt seitwärts zu Ihnen, als suche sie einen Ausweg aus der Szene.

Achten Sie auf den jungen Mann, der sich zu ihr beugt, ihre Hand hält und sie zum Trinken drängt. Ist das eine einfache Geste des Werbens oder etwas Berechnenderes? Im Hintergrund ist ein zweiter Mann hinter einem Tisch mit Weinkrug und Obst eingeschlafen. Vielleicht ist er ein betrunkener Ehemann, der die Verführung direkt vor seinen Augen nicht bemerkt.

Sehen Sie genauer auf die Wand hinter ihnen. Im Schatten hängt das dunkle Bildnis eines Mannes, dessen Blick wie eine stumme Mahnung wirkt. Noch unauffälliger ist das Bleiglasfenster links. Wenn Sie das Wappen in der Mitte betrachten, erkennen Sie die Allegorie der Temperantia, der Tugend der Mäßigung.

Vermeer lässt das wahre Wesen dieser Begegnung offen. Ist das Getränk im Glas einfacher Wein oder ein Aphrodisiakum, worauf die Zitrusfrüchte auf dem Tisch hindeuten? Während Sie hier stehen, sind Sie der einzige Zeuge dieses privaten Dramas, zwischen dem schlafenden Mann, dem wachenden Bildnis und dem verlegenen Blick des Mädchens.

text:
Take a moment to look at this scene from 1658, painted by Johannes Vermeer. At first glance, you see a young woman in a luminous red dress, but as you look closer, you will find a story unfolding through a series of mysterious clues.

Notice the young man leaning toward her, holding her hand as if urging her to drink. Then, look toward the back left corner. Do you see the second man? He appears to have fallen asleep, perhaps exhausted by the drink. This creates a tension in the room: is the young man acting for himself, or on behalf of the sleeping man?

Now, search for the details that are easy to miss. Look at the wall behind them for a dark portrait of a man. Is he a husband watching over the scene in admonition, or is he the identity of the man asleep in the corner? If you look to the left, there is a leaded glass window featuring a coat of arms. This is actually an allegory for Temperance, one of the cardinal virtues, providing a sharp contrast to the scene of seduction taking place.

Vermeer leaves us with several questions. Was the liquid in the glass simple wine, or something more provocative, suggested by the citrus fruits on the table? As you move on, consider how these hidden symbols change the meaning of the painting. Which character do you think holds the most power in this room?

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Take a moment to let your eyes wander through this scene by Johannes Vermeer, painted around 1659. You are looking at a high-stakes social puzzle. Notice the luminous red of the girl's dress; it is a bold, striking contrast to the muted tones of the room, pulling you immediately into her world.

But look closer at the tension. A young man leans in, urging her to drink, while she glances toward you with a look of embarrassment. Is he acting on his own, or for the man slumped in the background? This mystery is central to the painting's allure. Is the sleeping man a drunken husband, oblivious to the seduction? Or is the dark portrait on the wall the true authority, watching over the scene in silent admonition?

Keep an eye out for the subtle clues Vermeer left behind. Notice the citrus fruits on the table—a hint that the drink might be an aphrodisiac rather than simple wine. Then, look to the window. In the stained glass, you will find the allegory of Temperance, a cardinal virtue that stands in ironic contrast to the temptation unfolding in the room.

From its acquisition by the Duke of Brunswick in 1696 to its recent appearance on a German postage stamp, this work continues to captivate. As you move on, remember that this image is a masterclass in storytelling through detail, where every shadow and object invites a new theory.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted between 1658 and 1659, this interior scene is a masterful exercise in tension and symbolic layering. While the luminous red of the girl's dress immediately draws the eye, the painting's true depth lies in the details that invite a closer, more analytical gaze.

Notice the composition. A young man leans in, urging the girl to drink, while a second man slumbers in the background beside a silver plate of fruit. The central question is one of intent: is the young man acting for himself, or on behalf of the sleeping figure? The girl's sideways glance toward us suggests a moment of embarrassment or hesitation.

Look closely at the background. A dark portrait of a man hangs on the wall, casting a watchful eye over the scene. Is this an absent husband offering a silent admonition, or perhaps the drunken husband in the corner, now blind to the seduction? The nature of the drink itself is a point of debate; the presence of citrus fruits suggests it may be an aphrodisiac rather than simple wine.

For a final clue, examine the leaded glass window on the left. Within the coat of arms, you can find an allegory of Temperantia, the virtue of temperance. This inclusion creates a sharp, ironic contrast with the scene unfolding in the room. Once owned by the Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, this work remains a compelling study in the subtle psychological games of the Dutch Golden Age.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted between 1658 and 1659 by the Dutch master Johannes Vermeer, this scene captures a moment of high tension and hidden stories. As you look at the painting, you will see a young girl in a luminous red dress, which immediately draws the eye. She holds a wine glass while a young man leans in, holding her hand and urging her to drink. 

The composition is filled with intriguing details for you to discover. In the background, a second man has fallen asleep at a table covered with fruit and a wine jug. On the wall hangs a dark portrait of a man who seems to be watching the scene, and to the left, a leaded glass window features a coat of arms representing Temperance, one of the cardinal virtues.

The painting is a study in contrasting moods. While the young man attempts to seduce the woman, she looks toward us with an expression of embarrassment. Is the sleeping man a drunken husband, blind to the seduction, or is the man in the portrait the husband watching over his wife?

This work is a centerpiece of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum and remains one of Vermeer's most captivating genre pictures. It is a piece that invites us to question the motives of every character in the room. As a group, take a moment to look at the girl's expression and the sleeping man; what do you think is really happening in this room?

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted between 1658 and 1659, this genre scene by Johannes Vermeer invites a close look at the tension between its figures. In the foreground, a young woman in a luminous red dress holds a wine glass, while a man leans toward her, holding her hand as if urging her to drink. In the background, a second man sits slumped in a corner, appearing to have fallen asleep.

Notice the contrast in the palette; the woman’s dress is the focal point, while the men's pale clothing blends into the room's neutral tones. Look closely at the details: a silver plate with fruit and a wine jug sit on a table, and a dark portrait of a man hangs on the wall, watching the scene. To the left, a leaded glass window features a colored coat of arms depicting Temperantia, the allegory of Temperance.

The painting is a study in ambiguity. Is the man attempting to seduce the woman for himself or on behalf of the sleeping figure? Is the sleeping man a drunken husband, oblivious to the scene, while the portrait on the wall serves as a moral admonition? Even the drink is a mystery—it could be wine or an aphrodisiac, suggested by the citrus fruits.

Since the late 17th century, this work has been part of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum's collection. As you observe the interaction between the three figures, consider the social dynamics at play and the subtle warnings embedded in the room's details.

title: The Girl with the Wine Glass
text:
Painted between 1658 and 1659, this oil on canvas is a masterclass in composition and psychological tension. Vermeer, a titan of the Dutch Golden Age, creates a striking visual contrast by dressing the central figure in a luminous red that commands the viewer's attention, while the men fade into the pale, muted tones of the room.

The scene is a sophisticated puzzle of social dynamics. A young man leans in, urging the girl to drink, while a second man slumbers in the background. This creates a rich field for interpretation: is the sleeping man a drunken husband, oblivious to a seduction taking place under his nose? Is the dark portrait on the wall an admonishing husband watching from beyond the frame?

Note the subtle inclusion of the leaded glass window, which features a coat of arms depicting Temperance, one of the cardinal virtues. This creates a sharp, ironic tension between the virtue of moderation and the implied indulgence of the scene. This discourse on desire and restraint is exactly what makes Vermeer's work so enduring.

The painting's prestige is reflected in its provenance, having been acquired around 1696 by Anton Ulrich, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg. It remains a cornerstone of the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum. From its placement in a renowned Dresden exhibition to its feature on a German postage stamp, the work continues to be a primary example of Vermeer's ability to blend domesticity with profound human drama.

title: Self-Portrait as David
text:
Take a close look at this young man. He gazes directly at you, beardless with long dark hair, wearing a green doublet and a metallic cuirass. Notice the mirror-like sheen on his right shoulder. It is a striking image, but there is a mystery here: why is this called Self-Portrait as David?

As you look at the canvas, you will find no biblical symbols. This is because the painting is a fragment of a larger whole. It was cut down at the sides and bottom centuries ago. An etching from 1650 reveals what is missing: Giorgione originally depicted himself holding the severed head of Goliath.

Consider the boldness of this choice. Giorgione came from a poor background, yet he chose to cast himself as a biblical king and conqueror. By doing so, he created what is likely the first allegorical self-portrait in European art, using a myth to assert his own importance and skill.

The painting's history is as fragmented as its frame. For years, it was misidentified as a work by Raphael or Dosso Dossi. It even captivated the writer Samuel Beckett, who visited this museum in 1936.

As you study the dark browns and sienna of the skin, ask yourself: how does this change your perception of the artist knowing he died of the plague only a few months after completing this work? He left us not just a likeness, but a puzzle of ambition and loss.

Bedenken Sie die Kühnheit dieser Wahl. Giorgione stammte aus armen Verhältnissen und gab sich doch die Rolle eines biblischen Königs und Siegers. Die Geschichte des Gemäldes ist so bruchstückhaft wie sein Format. Jahrelang hielt man es fälschlich für ein Werk Raffaels oder Dosso Dossis. Es fesselte sogar den Schriftsteller Samuel Beckett, der dieses Museum 1936 besuchte.

Während Sie die dunklen Brauntöne und das Siena der Haut betrachten, fragen Sie sich: Wie verändert sich Ihr Bild des Künstlers, wenn Sie wissen, dass er nur wenige Monate nach Vollendung dieses Werks an der Pest starb? title: Self-Portrait as David
text:
Take a look at this striking young man. This is a self-portrait by the Venetian artist Giorgione, painted around 1510, shortly before he died of the plague.

Notice the details you can see together: his long dark hair, his direct gaze, and the metallic sheen of the armor over his green jacket. While it looks like a simple portrait today, there is a hidden story here. The painting was originally much larger and has been cut down over the centuries. It was actually a daring piece of roleplay; Giorgione painted himself as the biblical hero, King David, holding the severed head of Goliath.

By casting himself as a king and a conqueror, Giorgione—who came from a poor background—was using a biblical myth to tell the world about his own importance and skill as an artist. This makes it one of the first allegorical self-portraits in European history. Even the famous writer Samuel Beckett was captivated by this image when he visited this museum in 1936.

As you look at the painting now, you can no longer see the head of Goliath or the rest of the scene, leaving us with only this confident, beardless face.

Since the original image of victory was lost and only this gaze remains, how do you think the mood of the painting changes? Does he still seem like a triumphant king, or does he look like something else to you?

title: Self-Portrait as David
text:
You are looking at a painting by the mysterious Venetian master Giorgione, created just months before his untimely death during a plague outbreak. This is not just a portrait; it is widely considered the first allegorical self-portrait in the history of European art.

By depicting himself as the biblical King David, Giorgione performed a bold act of self-promotion. Born into poverty, he used this myth to confidently claim his own importance and skill as an artist, comparing himself to a legendary hero.

The painting you see today is actually a fragment of a larger, more dramatic scene. It was cut down centuries ago, removing the head of Goliath that the artist once held. We only know the original, shocking composition thanks to the writings of the famous biographer Giorgio Vasari and a 17th-century etching.

Its power continues to resonate far beyond the art world. This image has captivated legendary figures across history, influencing the works of the Nobel Prize-winning writer Samuel Beckett, who visited this museum specifically to see this piece.

As you admire the metallic sheen of the armor and the artist's direct gaze, remember that you are facing one of the most influential figures of the Venetian Renaissance in a work that redefined how artists portray themselves. It is a definitive highlight of the collection and a pivotal moment in the evolution of Western art.

text:
Executed in oil on canvas, this work is a pivotal example of early allegorical self-portraiture. Technically, Giorgione employs a palette of dark browns, ochres, and siennas, with sophisticated metallic reflections on the cuirass's right shoulder. The composition is now a tight crop of a young man in three-quarter profile, though this is the result of significant alteration.

Provenance and attribution research reveals the painting was cut down at the sides and bottom between 1650 and 1737. We know the original composition through a 1650 etching by Wenceslaus Hollar, which depicts the artist as David holding the head of Goliath. This scholarly reconstruction, confirmed in 1908 by Carl Justi and Franz Wickhoff, aligns with Giorgio Vasari's 1566 account of seeing the work in a Venetian palazzo. Vasari’s subsequent sketch served as the model for Giorgione's portrait in the 1568 edition of Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors and Architects.

Historically, the work represents a bold professional statement. By casting himself as the biblical king, Giorgione—who came from a poor background—used allegory to assert his skill and importance, marking a shift in European art history. The painting's influence extends into the 20th century, notably impacting Samuel Beckett. For further study of the artist's late period, a secondary version of this portrait, likely executed by a pupil, is held in the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest.

In Öl auf Leinwand ausgeführt, ist dieses Werk ein zentrales Beispiel des frühen allegorischen Selbstbildnisses. Technisch verwendet Giorgione eine Palette aus dunklen Braun-, Ocker- und Sienatönen, mit raffinierten metallischen Reflexen auf der rechten Schulter des Kürasses. Die Komposition zeigt heute einen engen Ausschnitt mit einem jungen Mann im Viertelprofil, doch dies ist das Ergebnis erheblicher Veränderungen.

Die Forschung zu Provenienz und Zuschreibung zeigt, dass das Gemälde zwischen 1650 und 1737 an den Seiten und unten beschnitten wurde. Die ursprüngliche Komposition kennen wir aus einer Radierung von Wenzel Hollar aus dem Jahr 1650, die den Künstler als David mit dem Haupt Goliaths zeigt. Diese wissenschaftliche Rekonstruktion, 1908 von Carl Justi und Franz Wickhoff bestätigt, deckt sich mit Giorgio Vasaris Bericht, er habe das Werk 1566 in einem venezianischen Palazzo gesehen. Vasaris anschließende Skizze diente als Vorlage für das Bildnis Giorgiones in der Ausgabe von 1568 der Lebensbeschreibungen der hervorragendsten Maler, Bildhauer und Architekten.

Historisch steht das Werk für eine kühne künstlerische Selbstbehauptung. Indem er sich als biblischen König darstellte, nutzte Giorgione, der aus armen Verhältnissen stammte, die Allegorie, um sein Können und seine Bedeutung zu behaupten, ein Wendepunkt in der europäischen Kunstgeschichte. Der Einfluss des Gemäldes reicht bis ins 20. Jahrhundert, besonders auf Samuel Beckett. Zum weiteren Studium der letzten Schaffenszeit des Künstlers: Eine zweite Fassung dieses Bildnisses, wahrscheinlich von einem Schüler ausgeführt, befindet sich im Szépművészeti Múzeum in Budapest.

text:

Notice how he emerges from a void of dark browns, with no room or landscape to distract you, leaving only the intimacy of this human connection.

Observe the soft play of light across his beardless face, rendered in warm ochres and siennas. Let your eyes follow the subtle metallic sheen of his armor, a bright contrast to the deep green of his doublet. There is a profound silence here, a sense of a moment frozen in time.

This is a man who chose to envision himself as the biblical David. By stepping into the role of the hero, he invites us to reflect on our own inner strength and the hidden depths of our identities. Consider the courage it takes to see oneself not as the world defines us, but as we aspire to be.

As you linger in the presence of this gaze, allow the noise of the outside world to fade away. What does this expression of confidence and vulnerability evoke within you? In this quiet space, perhaps you can find a reflection of your own resilience or a moment of peace. Let the simplicity of the composition breathe, and simply be present with the artist across the centuries.

title: Self-Portrait as David
text:
Take a moment to look at the young man before you. With his beardless face, long dark hair, and a steady gaze directed right at you, this is the Venetian painter Giorgione. He is dressed in a green doublet and a metallic cuirass that catches the light on the shoulder, rendered in a palette of deep browns, ochre, and sienna.

You might wonder why this is titled Self-Portrait as David, as there is no obvious biblical reference here. The truth is that this canvas has been physically altered. It was cut down at the sides and bottom centuries ago, removing the elements that would have identified him as the biblical king. We know what is missing thanks to a 1650 etching by Wenceslaus Hollar, which shows Giorgione holding the head of Goliath.

By depicting himself as David, Giorgione—who came from a poor background—was making a bold statement. He used this biblical myth as an allegory to assert his own skill and importance, making this likely the first allegorical self-portrait in European art history. It is a poignant image, as the artist died shortly after completing it, likely of the plague. This painting later captured the imagination of the writer Samuel Beckett, who visited this museum in 1936 and wrote specifically about this encounter with the artist's gaze.

text:

This canvas was cut down centuries ago, removing the sides and bottom. We know from a 17th-century etching and the writings of Giorgio Vasari that Giorgione originally painted himself holding the severed head of Goliath.

As you look at the artist's confident expression, consider this: Giorgione died shortly after completing this work, likely of the plague. Does knowing that this was one of his final statements change how you see his expression?

text:
Take a close look at this striking image. This is a self-portrait by the Venetian master Giorgione, and it contains a secret that makes it one of the most daring pieces in the museum. 

While you see a young man in a metallic cuirass, the painting is titled "Self-Portrait as David." Why? Because this canvas was once much larger. It was cut down centuries ago, removing the most shocking detail: the head of Goliath. By depicting himself as the biblical king, Giorgione—who came from a poor background—was making a bold, unprecedented claim about his own importance and skill. This is widely considered the first allegorical self-portrait in European art history.

The painting's mystery deepened over time. It was once misattributed to Raphael and Dosso Dossi before scholars used a 17th-century etching to rediscover its true identity. 

Beyond the art world, this image sparked the imagination of legendary writers. Samuel Beckett visited this very museum in 1936 and wrote about this specific work in his letters. 

As you move on, keep in mind the tragedy behind the brush: Giorgione died, likely of the plague, only a few months after completing this portrait. It stands as a final, confident statement of an artist who knew exactly how he wanted to be remembered. Now, look again at that mirror-like sheen on the shoulder—a masterclass in oil technique that continues to captivate visitors today.

text:
This oil on canvas is a rare and provocative piece by the Venetian master Giorgione, painted shortly before his death from the plague around 1510. At first glance, we see a young, beardless man with long dark hair, gazing directly at us. Note the contrast between the earthy browns and sienna of the skin and the mirror-like metallic sheen of the cuirass over his green doublet.

The title, Self-Portrait as David, is a puzzle because the painting has been cut down at the sides and bottom. In its original state, Giorgione depicted himself as the biblical King David holding the head of Goliath. This was a bold move; coming from a poor background, Giorgione used this biblical myth as an allegory to assert his own skill and importance. It is considered one of the first allegorical self-portraits in European art.

The work's history is as complex as its composition. For years, it was misattributed to Raphael and Dosso Dossi before being correctly identified as Giorgione's work. Its original composition was only rediscovered in 1908 through a 17th-century etching by Wenceslaus Hollar. This painting also served as the model for the portrait of the artist in Giorgio Vasari’s influential "Lives of the Most Excellent Painters."

If you look closely at the figure's expression and the way he presents himself, you can see the confidence of the artist. A question to consider: how does the removal of the head of Goliath change your perception of the man before you?

title: Self-Portrait as David
text:
This oil on canvas is a rare and pivotal moment in European art history. While it now appears as a simple portrait of a young man with long dark hair and a metallic cuirass, it is actually the first allegorical self-portrait of its kind. 

The painting’s current state is a fragment of its original composition. It was cut down at the sides and bottom after 1650, removing the evidence of the biblical narrative. We know from a 1650 etching by Wenceslaus Hollar and the writings of Giorgio Vasari that Giorgione originally depicted himself as King David holding the head of Goliath. By casting himself as this biblical hero, the artist—who came from a poor background—used the myth as a bold allegory to assert his own skill and importance.

The work's identity was a subject of scholarly debate for centuries, once attributed to Raphael and Dosso Dossi before being correctly identified as Giorgione’s work. Its status as a "David" was only rediscovered in 1908 through the study of Hollar's etching.

The painting's magnetic quality is reflected in its influence on figures far beyond the art world, including the writer Samuel Beckett. The artist likely died of the plague only a few months after completing this work. To understand the progression of the artist's self-image, you may also wish to seek out the second version of this portrait, created by Giorgione or a pupil, which is held in the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest.

text:

As he worked, he changed his mind about the composition, physically enlarging the picture by attaching extra pieces of wood.

Now, let your eyes wander through the scene. Beyond the striking image of Judith and the severed head, can you spot the fragments of armor lingering in the background? These remnants remind us of the military power Judith managed to dismantle through a daring ruse. Notice the maidservant on the right; her burning candle does more than just light the room—it creates a dramatic tension, pulling your focus toward the severed head of the commander.

Consider the contrast in the figures: the vitality and strength radiating from the young Judith versus the aged maidservant. While this image captures the aftermath of the deed, Rubens actually painted a whole cycle of this story. Imagine the scene just moments before this one, where Holofernes' body rears up one last time, or the moment after, when the head is hidden in a sack to smuggle it from the camp. Why do you think Rubens kept this specific study in his studio for so long before it eventually found its way into a palace gallery?

Rubens likely created this piece for his own study rather than for a client. He kept it in his studio for a long time, experimenting with the composition as he worked. While the image is violent, Rubens depicts Judith as a figure of strength and vitality.

title: Judith with the Head of Holofernes
text:
Behold one of the most striking examples of the Flemish Baroque: Peter Paul Rubens' Judith with the Head of Holofernes. This painting is a masterclass in high drama and visceral power, capturing a pivotal moment from the Book of Judith. Rubens presents the heroine not just as a savior, but as a figure of immense strength and vitality, holding the severed head of the enemy commander by a tuft of hair.

What makes this piece a true insider's highlight is its origin. Unlike many of his grand commissions, Rubens likely created this for his own study. He worked on a simple wooden panel, changing the composition and physically enlarging the surface as he went. This gives us a rare, raw glimpse into the creative process of one of history's most influential artists. 

The impact of the work lies in its bold contrast: the sensual beauty of Judith set against the gruesome reality of the beheaded Holofernes, all illuminated by the flickering light of a maidservant's candle. It is a scene of triumph and terror that epitomizes the theatricality Rubens is famous for. As you move through the gallery, remember that this wasn't just a painting, but a laboratory for Rubens to refine his style. It stands as a definitive example of how Baroque art captures the peak of human emotion and conflict.

title: Judith with the Head of Holofernes
text:
Painted in Antwerp between 1616 and 1618, this work is a prime example of the Flemish Baroque. Of particular interest to the student of technique is the physical construction of the piece. Rubens likely produced this for study purposes rather than as a commission, evidenced by his use of a simple wooden panel rather than high-quality wood. The composition evolved organically in the studio; Rubens revised the arrangement several times, physically enlarging the painting surface by attaching additional pieces of wood.

The painting captures the climax of the biblical narrative from the Book of Judith. Rubens emphasizes a contrast in vitality, depicting Judith as a sensual, strong figure with her breast nearly bared, juxtaposed against the severed head of the Assyrian commander, Holofernes. The lighting is driven by the burning candle held by the maidservant, a classic Baroque device to create dramatic tension.

This work is part of a broader thematic exploration by Rubens. Around 1610, he painted a full-length depiction of the preceding moment—the initial stroke of the sword—a version of which is held in the National Museum in Warsaw. He also executed a subsequent scene showing the head concealed in a sack. Documented in the gallery of Salzdahlum Palace since approximately 1700, the painting now resides in the Herzog Anton Ulrich Museum. It serves as a vital record of Rubens' process, illustrating how he manipulated both the physical support and the composition to refine his vision of this recurring artistic motif.

Take a look at the central figure, Judith. Rubens depicts her as a powerful, sensual woman who has just saved her people from destruction. In one hand, she holds the sword used for the deed; in the other, she grips the severed head of Holofernes, the enemy commander, by a tuft of hair. Beside her, an old maidservant holds a burning candle that casts a sharp light across the scene.

The story comes from the Book of Judith. To save her besieged hometown of Bethulia, Judith used her beauty and wit to gain access to the enemy camp. After plying Holofernes with wine until he fell asleep, she killed him with his own sword.

As you explore the painting, notice the contrast between the strength of Judith and the lifeless head of the commander. You can even spot pieces of his armour discarded in the background. Interestingly, Rubens likely painted this for his own study rather than a commission, as he used a simple wooden panel and adjusted the composition as he worked.

Looking at the bold colors and the intense emotion on the faces, it is easy to see why this scene has been depicted by so many artists. Do you think the painting captures the triumph of the moment or the horror of the act?

Erlauben Sie sich, still zu werden und über den Mut nachzudenken, den es braucht, sich einer übermächtigen Gewalt entgegenzustellen. Lassen Sie in der Ruhe dieser Galerie die kräftigen Farben und die dramatische Komposition ein Gefühl des Triumphes über alle Widrigkeiten wecken. Lassen Sie sich vom Bild dazu anregen, über Ihre eigenen Quellen innerer Stärke nachzudenken und über die Momente, in denen eine einzige, entschlossene Tat den Lauf der Geschichte verändern kann.

Sie ist eine Gestalt der Entschlossenheit und Anmut, die gehandelt hat, um ihr Volk vor dem Untergang zu retten. Neben ihr streckt die alte Dienerin die Hand aus, ihr Ausdruck eine Mischung aus Ehrfurcht und Ernst.

Während Sie die Komposition betrachten, bedenken Sie den Gegensatz zwischen der Weichheit der Haut und der kalten Starre der Rüstung im Hintergrund. Diese Szene ist eine Studie der Spannung zwischen Schönheit und Grausamkeit, zwischen der Zerbrechlichkeit des Lebens und der Kraft der Überzeugung.

Atmen Sie durch und erlauben Sie sich, in der Stille dieser Begegnung ganz da zu sein. Denken Sie über das Gewicht des Augenblicks nach, den plötzlichen Übergang vom Chaos des Kampfes zu dieser stillen, schweren Zeit danach. Welche Gefühle steigen in Ihnen auf, wenn Sie der Heldin in die Augen sehen? Lassen Sie das Gemälde Ihre Aufmerksamkeit halten und laden Sie sich ein, über den Mut nachzudenken, den es braucht, sich einer großen Dunkelheit zu stellen, und über die stille Entschlossenheit, die nötig ist, um einen neuen Morgen herbeizuführen.
